elements.name: Hydrogen
elements.short: Low-carbon fuel and feedstock for fertiliser and steel. Not a greenhouse gas itself, but leaks extend methane's life in the air.

contexts.environmental: Hydrogen itself is not a greenhouse gas, but leaked hydrogen slows the breakdown of methane, so it warms indirectly.
contexts.engineering: Made mostly from natural gas today; electrolysis of water with renewable power is the low-carbon route. Storage and pipe embrittlement are the engineering problems.
contexts.geological: Bound in water, hydrocarbons and clay minerals; natural free hydrogen deposits are being explored.
contexts.chemical: Forms covalent bonds with almost everything; H⁺ sets pH. Flammable in air from about 4% to 75% by volume.
contexts.land: Land is needed for the wind and solar that make electrolytic hydrogen; storage salt caverns and pipelines bring planning questions.

briefing_text.nature: The most abundant element in the universe; on Earth mostly bound in water and organic matter. Free hydrogen is rare, though natural underground deposits exist.
briefing_text.climate: Not a greenhouse gas, but leaked hydrogen slows the breakdown of methane in the air, so it warms indirectly. Low-carbon hydrogen is promoted for steel, fertiliser, shipping and heavy transport.
briefing_text.pollution: Burning hydrogen gives water, but high-temperature combustion still forms nitrogen oxides. Making it from gas without carbon capture emits CO₂.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Used to make ammonia, refine oil and hydrogenate fats; produced mostly by steam reforming of natural gas, increasingly by electrolysis. Hydrogen is covered by EU CBAM.
briefing_text.health: Non-toxic; an asphyxiant only in enclosed spaces.
briefing_text.hazards: Extremely flammable (H220), burns with an almost invisible flame, leaks easily and embrittles some steels. UN1049 (compressed), UN1966 (refrigerated liquid).
briefing_text.discovery: Identified as an element by Henry Cavendish in 1766; named by Lavoisier from Greek for 'water-former'. Stable.

elements.name: Helium
elements.short: Inert, finite gas from natural gas fields. No climate or soil role; escapes to space once released.

contexts.environmental: Escapes to space once released, so supply is finite; no direct climate effect.
contexts.engineering: Liquid helium cools MRI magnets; used in welding shields and leak detection.
contexts.geological: Produced by radioactive decay of uranium and thorium and trapped in natural gas fields.
contexts.chemical: A noble gas: no stable compounds. Asphyxiant in confined spaces.
contexts.land: Little land footprint; extraction is tied to gas fields.

briefing_text.nature: Second most abundant element in the universe but rare on Earth; made by radioactive decay underground and trapped in some natural gas fields.
briefing_text.climate: No climate effect. Released helium escapes to space, so supply is finite.
briefing_text.pollution: None of note.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Cooling for MRI scanners and research magnets, leak testing, welding shield gas, semiconductor making and balloons.
briefing_text.health: Non-toxic; breathing pure helium causes asphyxiation.
briefing_text.hazards: Gas under pressure; liquid helium causes cold burns and expands violently. UN1046 (compressed), UN1963 (refrigerated liquid).
briefing_text.discovery: Seen in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 (Janssen, Lockyer) before it was found on Earth in 1895 (Ramsay). Named from Greek 'helios', the Sun. Stable.

elements.name: Lithium
elements.short: Battery metal of the energy transition. Brine and rock mining strain water and land; spent batteries are a fire risk at waste sites.

contexts.environmental: Brine and hard-rock mining use water and energy; battery recycling recovers lithium.
contexts.engineering: Lithium-ion batteries for vehicles and grid storage; also glass, ceramics and greases.
contexts.geological: Found in pegmatites (spodumene) and salt-lake brines; on the UK critical minerals list.
contexts.chemical: Reactive alkali metal; reacts with water to give hydrogen. Lithium salts are used in medicine.
contexts.land: Mine sites and evaporation ponds take large areas; battery fires are a waste-site risk.

briefing_text.nature: Present in pegmatite rocks, clays and salt-lake brines; traces in seawater and some mineral springs.
briefing_text.climate: Central to lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles and grid storage. Hard-rock lithium refining is energy intensive.
briefing_text.pollution: Brine extraction draws down water in arid regions; mine wastes and battery fires at waste sites are growing concerns.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Batteries, ceramics and glass, lubricating greases, aluminium alloys. On the UK critical minerals list.
briefing_text.health: Lithium salts are a medicine for bipolar disorder, with a narrow safe dose range.
briefing_text.hazards: The metal reacts with water to release hydrogen (H260) and burns fiercely. Lithium batteries are dangerous goods (UN3480, UN3481, UN3090, UN3091).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered in 1817 by Johan Arfwedson; named from Greek 'lithos', stone. Stable.

elements.name: Beryllium
elements.short: Rare aerospace metal. No soil or climate role of note; its dust causes chronic lung disease and cancer.

contexts.environmental: Rare in the environment; airborne dust from processing is the concern.
contexts.engineering: Copper-beryllium alloys for non-sparking tools and springs; aerospace and X-ray windows.
contexts.geological: Found in beryl and bertrandite; emerald and aquamarine are beryl.
contexts.chemical: Beryllium compounds cause chronic beryllium disease and are carcinogens; tight exposure limits apply.
contexts.land: Contaminated land is possible at old aerospace and electronics sites.

briefing_text.nature: Rare; found in beryl (emerald, aquamarine) and bertrandite.
briefing_text.climate: Minor; used in some aerospace and nuclear components.
briefing_text.pollution: Dust from machining and processing is the concern; little enters the wider environment.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Copper-beryllium alloys for springs and non-sparking tools, X-ray windows, aerospace and defence parts.
briefing_text.health: Beryllium dust causes chronic beryllium disease and is a human carcinogen. Strict workplace controls apply.
briefing_text.hazards: Carc. 1B; acutely toxic by inhalation. UN1567 (beryllium powder).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered in beryl by Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1798; isolated in 1828. Stable.

elements.name: Boron
elements.short: Plant micronutrient needed by brassicas and beet. Used in insulation glass fibre and wind-turbine magnets; boric acid harms fertility.

contexts.environmental: Plants need trace boron; too much in irrigation water is toxic.
contexts.engineering: Borosilicate glass, fibreglass insulation, neodymium magnets and nuclear control rods.
contexts.geological: Mined as borates (borax) from evaporite deposits.
contexts.chemical: Forms covalent boron–oxygen compounds; boric acid is a reproductive toxicant.
contexts.land: Boron deficiency shows in brassicas and beet; fertiliser trace element.

briefing_text.nature: Found as borates in evaporite deposits; plants need small amounts.
briefing_text.climate: Used in glass-fibre insulation and in NdFeB magnets for wind turbines and motors.
briefing_text.pollution: Boron in some effluents and irrigation water can harm crops.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Borosilicate glass, fibreglass, detergents, ceramics, magnets and nuclear control rods.
briefing_text.health: Boric acid and borax are classed as toxic to reproduction.
briefing_text.hazards: Boric acid and borates: Repr. 1B. Boron powder is flammable.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated in 1808 by Gay-Lussac and Thénard, and by Humphry Davy; name from borax. Stable.

elements.name: Carbon
elements.short: The element we count: CO₂ and methane drive warming. Soils and peat store more carbon than the air; soot and carbon monoxide harm health.

contexts.environmental: Carbon dioxide and methane are the two largest causes of human-made warming. In Northern Ireland in 2023, carbon dioxide made up 61.5% of greenhouse gas emissions and methane 30.2%. Soils, peat and forests hold far more carbon than the air, and can lose it fast when drained or ploughed.
contexts.engineering: Carbon is the backbone of fuels, plastics, steel (as the reducing agent and alloying element), cement chemistry (limestone) and carbon fibre. Graphite is a battery anode material and is on the UK critical minerals list. Carbon capture aims to keep CO₂ from industrial sources out of the air.
contexts.geological: Carbon is stored in limestone and chalk (the largest store), coal, oil, gas, peat and diamonds. Northern Ireland has chalk and limestone, lignite near Lough Neagh, and extensive blanket and raised bogs.
contexts.chemical: Group 14, period 2. Carbon forms four bonds and long chains and rings with itself, giving millions of organic compounds. Forms include graphite, diamond, graphene and fullerenes. Carbon-14 dating uses its radioactive isotope.
contexts.land: Agriculture produced 31.4% of Northern Ireland's emissions in 2024, mostly methane from cattle and sheep. Peat soils store a large share of Northern Ireland's land carbon; drained peat is a net source of CO₂. Soil carbon is measured slowly and is easy to lose.

briefing_text.nature: In every living thing, in limestone and chalk, coal, oil, gas, peat and diamonds, and as CO₂ and methane in the air.
briefing_text.climate: Carbon dioxide and methane are the two largest causes of human-made warming. Soils and peat hold more carbon than the air.
briefing_text.pollution: Soot (black carbon), carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds harm health; plastics are carbon-based pollution.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Fuels, plastics, steel (as reducer and alloy), cement chemistry, carbon black, graphite, carbon fibre.
briefing_text.health: Elemental carbon is low in toxicity; carbon monoxide poisons, and fine soot damages lungs and heart.
briefing_text.hazards: See the carbon briefing safety tab: CO₂, CO, methane, carbon dusts and self-heating charcoal.
briefing_text.discovery: Known since prehistory as charcoal and soot; recognised as an element by Lavoisier in the 1780s; name from Latin 'carbo', charcoal. Stable (carbon-14 is radioactive, half-life 5,730 years).

safety.coshh: COSHH applies to carbon dusts (carbon black, graphite, coal) and to carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. Most deaths come from carbon monoxide (combustion in poorly ventilated spaces) and from CO₂ build-up in cellars, silos and slurry stores.
classes: Carbon: graphite, diamond
Not classified.
Carbon black
No harmonised CLP classification; IARC Group 2B. Combustible dust.
Activated carbon and charcoal
May be self-heating (class 4.2 for transport) depending on test results.
wels: 10 mg/m³ LTEL inhalable; 4 mg/m³ LTEL respirable
un: Carbon, animal or vegetable origin (e.g. charcoal)
safety.risks: Elemental carbon is low in toxicity, but its dusts can explode and charcoal can self-heat in storage. Carbon monoxide gives no warning. Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects in pits and slurry tanks; dry ice in a vehicle or cold room can reach dangerous levels.

manufacturing: cement; covered by EU and UK CBAM
almost all made from fossil carbon
climate: GWP 1 by definition; lasts centuries to millennia
100-year GWP 28 (AR5, as used in the UK inventory); lasts about 12 years
warms by absorbing sunlight and darkening snow
not a direct greenhouse gas, but extends methane's life

elements.name: Nitrogen
elements.short: Grass's main nutrient and Northern Ireland's main air and water pollutant from farming: ammonia, nitrate and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide.

contexts.environmental: Nitrogen gas is harmless, but reactive nitrogen is not. Ammonia from slurry and fertiliser damages peat bogs, woodland and lichens; nitrate leaches into water; nitrous oxide is a powerful greenhouse gas; and nitrogen oxides from engines harm lungs. DAERA reports that 97% of Northern Ireland's ammonia comes from agriculture.
contexts.engineering: The Haber–Bosch process turns nitrogen from air and hydrogen from natural gas into ammonia, which becomes most of the world's fertiliser. It is energy intensive; fertilisers are covered by EU CBAM and will be covered by UK CBAM. Ammonia is also proposed as a shipping fuel and hydrogen carrier.
contexts.geological: Most of the Earth's nitrogen is in the atmosphere as N₂. Rocks hold little. Natural nitrate deposits exist in deserts such as Chile's Atacama.
contexts.chemical: Group 15, period 2. The triple bond in N₂ makes it very unreactive, which is why fixing nitrogen takes either lightning, bacteria in clover roots, or an industrial plant. Reactive forms include ammonia (NH₃), ammonium (NH₄⁺), nitrate (NO₃⁻), nitrous oxide (N₂O) and nitrogen oxides (NOₓ).
contexts.land: Grassland in Northern Ireland runs on nitrogen from slurry, fertiliser and clover. The Nutrients Action Programme limits how much manure nitrogen can be applied and when. Ammonia drifts from farms onto designated sites, which is why planning applications for livestock housing are assessed for ammonia.

briefing_text.nature: 78% of the air as N₂; fixed into soil by lightning and by bacteria in clover and other legumes.
briefing_text.climate: Nitrous oxide is a powerful, long-lived greenhouse gas; ammonia and nitrogen oxides affect air quality and ozone.
briefing_text.pollution: Ammonia damages habitats; nitrate pollutes water; nitrogen oxides harm lungs.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Ammonia and nitrogen fertilisers, nitric acid, explosives, nylon, and nitrogen gas for food packaging and inerting.
briefing_text.health: Nitrogen gas is inert but asphyxiates in confined spaces; nitrogen dioxide and ammonia irritate lungs.
briefing_text.hazards: See the nitrogen briefing safety tab.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated in 1772 by Daniel Rutherford; named from Greek for 'nitre-former'. Stable.

safety.coshh: Nitrogen gas is not toxic, but it is a simple asphyxiant: in a confined space it displaces oxygen without warning. COSHH applies to the nitrogen compounds below, and confined-space rules apply to nitrogen gas.
classes: Nitrogen, compressed gas
Press. Gas H280 (contains gas under pressure; may explode if heated). No harmonised CLP entry; this is the supplier classification.
Nitrogen, refrigerated liquid
Press. Gas H281 (contains refrigerated gas; may cause cryogenic burns).
wels: No WEL: an asphyxiant. Control is by keeping oxygen above safe levels.
safety.risks: Nitrogen gas causes asphyxiation in tanks, silos and cold rooms; liquid nitrogen causes cold burns and expands about 700 times as it boils. Ammonium nitrate fertiliser is an oxidiser and must be stored away from fuel and organic matter.

nature: proteins in grass, manure and soil organic matter
manufacturing: made by Haber–Bosch; the root of nearly all nitrogen fertiliser
solid fertiliser; protected urea cuts ammonia loss
Ammonium nitrate and calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN)
the main straight nitrogen fertilisers in the UK and Ireland
made from ammonia; its production emits nitrous oxide
another industrial source of nitrous oxide
climate: a greenhouse gas with a 100-year global warming potential of 265 (AR5, as used in the UK inventory)
not a greenhouse gas, but it re-deposits and part of it is later emitted as N₂O
form ground-level ozone, itself a greenhouse gas

elements.name: Oxygen
elements.short: Makes up 21% of the air. Ozone shields us high up but is a pollutant and greenhouse gas near the ground; low oxygen kills fish in rivers.

contexts.environmental: Ozone (O₃) shields the Earth from UV high up but is a pollutant and greenhouse gas at ground level.
contexts.engineering: Used in steelmaking, medicine, water treatment and oxy-fuel combustion.
contexts.geological: The most abundant element in the Earth's crust, bound in silicates and oxides.
contexts.chemical: Highly reactive oxidiser; most elements form oxides. Oxygen-enriched air raises fire risk.
contexts.land: Dissolved oxygen in rivers falls when nutrients cause algal blooms, killing fish.

briefing_text.nature: 21% of the air and nearly half the Earth's crust by mass, bound in water, silicates and oxides.
briefing_text.climate: Ozone (O₃) protects from UV in the stratosphere but is a greenhouse gas and pollutant near the ground.
briefing_text.pollution: Ground-level ozone forms from traffic and industrial emissions in sunlight; low oxygen in rivers kills fish.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Steelmaking, medicine, water treatment, welding and cutting, oxy-fuel combustion; separated from air.
briefing_text.health: Essential for breathing; high concentrations over long periods can damage lungs.
briefing_text.hazards: Oxidiser: oxygen-enriched air makes fires burn fiercely. UN1072 (compressed), UN1073 (refrigerated liquid).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Carl Scheele (about 1772) and Joseph Priestley (1774); named by Lavoisier. Stable.

elements.name: Fluorine
elements.short: Source of F-gas refrigerants (powerful greenhouse gases) and PFAS 'forever chemicals'. Fluoride reaches soil in phosphate fertiliser.

contexts.environmental: Fluorine's carbon compounds are the problem: hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and other F-gases are powerful greenhouse gases, and PFAS ('forever chemicals') persist in water, soil and blood. Fluoride also enters soils as an impurity in phosphate fertiliser.
contexts.engineering: Fluorspar (calcium fluoride) is turned into hydrogen fluoride, the starting point for refrigerants, PTFE, lithium battery salts, uranium enrichment and aluminium smelting. Northern Ireland follows the EU F-gas Regulation (EU) 2024/573 under the Windsor Framework; Great Britain still applies its retained 2014-based regime.
contexts.geological: Fluorine occurs as fluorspar (fluorite), in cryolite and in fluoroapatite, the main mineral of phosphate rock. Natural fluoride in groundwater varies with geology.
contexts.chemical: Group 17, period 2. The most electronegative and most reactive element; it reacts with almost everything, including glass. The carbon–fluorine bond is the strongest single bond in organic chemistry, which is why PFAS do not break down.
contexts.land: Northern Ireland's public water supply is not artificially fluoridated (NI Water, January 2025); Ireland's has been since 1964. Land contaminated by firefighting foam at airports, fire-training grounds and some industrial sites is the main PFAS land issue.

briefing_text.nature: Fluorspar, cryolite and the fluoroapatite in phosphate rock; fluoride in some groundwater.
briefing_text.climate: F-gases (HFCs, SF₆, NF₃) are powerful, long-lived greenhouse gases.
briefing_text.pollution: PFAS 'forever chemicals' persist in water, soil and blood; fluoride enters soil with phosphate fertiliser.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Refrigerants, fluoropolymers such as PTFE, battery salts, aluminium smelting, uranium enrichment.
briefing_text.health: Fluoride protects teeth in small amounts and harms teeth and bone in excess; some PFAS are linked to health effects.
briefing_text.hazards: See the fluorine briefing safety tab.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Henri Moissan in 1886, after attempts that injured or killed several chemists; name from fluorspar. Stable.

safety.coshh: COSHH applies. Fluorine gas and hydrogen fluoride are among the most hazardous industrial chemicals; hydrofluoric acid burns may not hurt at first but can be fatal. Anyone handling them needs specific first aid (calcium gluconate) on site.
classes: Fluorine (gas)
Ox. Gas 1 H270 (may cause or intensify fire); Press. Gas H280; Acute Tox. 2 H330 (fatal if inhaled); Skin Corr. 1A H314. Harmonised (CLP Annex VI).
safety.risks: Elemental fluorine is a pale yellow gas that is toxic, corrosive and ignites many materials on contact. It is handled only in specialist plant. Refrigerant gases are not toxic in normal use but displace oxygen in enclosed spaces and some are flammable (for example R-32 and the hydrocarbon alternatives).

nature: in phosphate rock; carries fluoride into fertilisers
climate: a breakdown product of some newer refrigerants, building up in water

elements.name: Neon
elements.short: Inert trace gas in the air. No climate, soil or health effect beyond asphyxiation in confined spaces.

contexts.environmental: No environmental effect of note.
contexts.engineering: Lighting, lasers and cryogenics; a by-product of air separation.
contexts.geological: A trace gas in the atmosphere.
contexts.chemical: A noble gas: no stable compounds.

briefing_text.nature: A trace gas in air (about 18 parts per million).
briefing_text.climate: No effect.
briefing_text.pollution: None.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Neon signs, lasers (including for chip lithography), cryogenics; a by-product of air separation.
briefing_text.health: Non-toxic; asphyxiant in confined spaces.
briefing_text.hazards: Gas under pressure. UN1065 (compressed), UN1913 (refrigerated liquid).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Ramsay and Travers in 1898; from Greek 'neos', new. Stable.

elements.name: Sodium
elements.short: Salt. Road salt raises chloride in streams and damages verges; too much in the diet raises blood pressure. Sodium-ion batteries are emerging.

contexts.environmental: Road salt raises chloride in streams; sodium in soils damages structure.
contexts.engineering: Sodium-ion batteries are emerging; sodium hydroxide and carbonate are bulk chemicals.
contexts.geological: Rock salt deposits, including those mined at Kilroot near Carrickfergus.
contexts.chemical: Metal reacts violently with water. Sodium salts are mostly soluble.
contexts.land: Salt on roads and spray near coasts affects verges and hedges.

briefing_text.nature: Seawater salt, rock salt and many minerals; the sixth most abundant element in the crust.
briefing_text.climate: Sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a lower-cost storage option; soda ash making emits CO₂.
briefing_text.pollution: Road salt raises chloride and sodium in streams and damages verges; salty soils lose structure.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Salt, caustic soda, soda ash for glass, sodium bicarbonate, de-icing; rock salt mined at Kilroot near Carrickfergus.
briefing_text.health: An essential nutrient; too much dietary salt raises blood pressure.
briefing_text.hazards: The metal reacts violently with water (H260). UN1428 (sodium).
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807 by electrolysis of caustic soda; symbol Na from Latin 'natrium'. Stable.

elements.name: Magnesium
elements.short: At the heart of chlorophyll. Low magnesium in spring grass causes grass tetany in cattle and sheep; magnesium-rich basalt can draw down CO₂.

contexts.environmental: Every chlorophyll molecule holds a magnesium atom, so no magnesium means no photosynthesis. Magnesium-rich rocks such as basalt and olivine absorb CO₂ slowly as they weather, which is the basis of 'enhanced rock weathering' as a carbon removal method, still at the research and trial stage.
contexts.engineering: Magnesium metal is a third lighter than aluminium and is alloyed for car parts, laptops and aircraft. Most is made in China by the Pidgeon process, which is energy and carbon intensive. Magnesium oxide is used in refractories, animal feed, cements and water treatment. Magnesium and magnesite are on the UK 2024 critical minerals list.
contexts.geological: Magnesium is the eighth most abundant element in the crust. It is found in dolomite, magnesite, olivine, serpentine and the basalts of the Antrim Plateau, and in seawater as magnesium chloride and sulfate.
contexts.chemical: Group 2, period 3; an alkaline earth metal. Burns with a dazzling white flame and keeps burning in carbon dioxide and steam, so water makes a magnesium fire worse. Forms Mg²⁺ ions in water.
contexts.land: Cattle and sheep cannot store magnesium. Fast-growing spring grass, high potassium and heavy nitrogen lower the magnesium cows take in, causing grass tetany (staggers), which can kill within hours. Magnesian (dolomitic) lime supplies magnesium as well as raising pH.

briefing_text.nature: Dolomite, magnesite, olivine, basalt and seawater; at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule.
briefing_text.climate: Magnesium-rich rocks absorb CO₂ as they weather; making the metal is carbon intensive.
briefing_text.pollution: Little pollution concern; dust and fume at work.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Light alloys, refractories, animal feed, fertiliser, de-icing salts and cements.
briefing_text.health: An essential nutrient; low magnesium in grazing cattle and sheep causes grass tetany.
briefing_text.hazards: See the magnesium briefing safety tab: powder and swarf are fire risks.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Humphry Davy in 1808; named from Magnesia, a district in Greece. Stable.

safety.coshh: COSHH applies to magnesium dust and fume and to magnesium oxide. The bigger risk is fire: magnesium powder and swarf are flammable and react with water to release hydrogen.
classes: Magnesium powder (pyrophoric)
Pyr. Sol. 1 H250; Water-react. 1 H260 (releases flammable gas with water). Harmonised (CLP Annex VI).
Magnesium powder or turnings (stabilised)
Flam. Sol. 1 H228; Water-react. 2 H261. Harmonised (CLP Annex VI).
Magnesium (massive metal)
Not classified in solid form, but it burns once alight.
wels: 10 mg/m³ LTEL inhalable dust; 4 mg/m³ LTEL respirable dust
un: Magnesium powder or magnesium alloys powder
Magnesium or magnesium alloys (>50% Mg) in pellets, turnings or ribbons
safety.risks: Never use water or a CO₂ extinguisher on burning magnesium; use dry sand or a Class D powder. Machining swarf and fine powder are the main fire risks in workshops. Magnesium compounds in fertiliser and feed are of low hazard.

nature: the green pigment in every leaf
magnesium silicates in basalts and ultramafic rocks
climate: releases process CO₂, as with limestone for cement
spreading crushed basalt or olivine on land to draw down CO₂; research stage

elements.name: Aluminium
elements.short: Energy-hungry metal covered by CBAM. In acid soils and water it turns toxic to roots and fish; liming locks it up.

contexts.environmental: Primary smelting uses huge amounts of electricity; recycling uses a small fraction of that energy.
contexts.engineering: Cans, window frames, vehicles and power lines. Aluminium is covered by EU and UK CBAM.
contexts.geological: Most abundant metal in the crust; bauxite is the ore.
contexts.chemical: Forms a protective oxide layer. Soluble aluminium is toxic to fish and roots in acid water.
contexts.land: In acid soils, aluminium becomes soluble and limits root growth; liming locks it up.

briefing_text.nature: The most abundant metal in the crust, in clays, feldspars and bauxite. Soluble only in acid conditions.
briefing_text.climate: Primary aluminium smelting uses large amounts of electricity and releases perfluorocarbons; recycling uses a small fraction of the energy. Covered by EU and UK CBAM.
briefing_text.pollution: Bauxite residue ('red mud') is a large waste stream; acid rain mobilises aluminium that kills fish.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Packaging, building frames, vehicles, power lines, cookware.
briefing_text.health: Low toxicity at normal exposure; aluminium in dialysis fluid once caused harm.
briefing_text.hazards: Powder is flammable and reacts with water (UN1396 uncoated, UN1309 coated). Massive metal is not classified.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Hans Christian Ørsted in 1825 and Friedrich Wöhler in 1827; 'aluminium' is the IUPAC spelling. Stable.

elements.name: Silicon
elements.short: Solar panels and chips. Respirable silica dust from cutting stone and concrete causes silicosis.

contexts.environmental: Respirable crystalline silica dust causes silicosis; a workplace, not a field, problem.
contexts.engineering: Solar panels, semiconductors, silicones and concrete aggregate.
contexts.geological: Second most abundant crustal element; quartz and silicate minerals.
contexts.chemical: Forms silicon–oxygen networks; silicones are silicon–oxygen polymers.
contexts.land: Quarrying for sand and gravel; silica in soils from weathered rock.

briefing_text.nature: Second most abundant element in the crust, in quartz, sand and silicate rocks.
briefing_text.climate: The base of solar panels; making metallurgical silicon is electricity and carbon intensive.
briefing_text.pollution: Respirable crystalline silica from cutting stone and concrete causes silicosis and lung cancer.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Solar cells, microchips, silicones, glass, concrete and aggregates, aluminium alloys.
briefing_text.health: Silicon itself is low in toxicity; respirable silica dust is the hazard.
briefing_text.hazards: Respirable crystalline silica WEL 0.1 mg/m³ (EH40). Silicon powder is flammable.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1824; from Latin 'silex', flint. Stable.

elements.name: Phosphorus
elements.short: Essential crop nutrient and the main cause of Lough Neagh's algal blooms. Northern Ireland's farms run a phosphorus surplus.

contexts.environmental: Phosphorus is the nutrient that limits plant and algal growth in most fresh water. Too much of it, washed or leached from farmland, slurry and sewage, feeds the algal blooms that have covered Lough Neagh. DAERA describes excess phosphorus as the main cause of poor water quality in Northern Ireland.
contexts.engineering: Mined phosphate rock is turned into fertiliser with sulfuric acid, making phosphoric acid and phosphogypsum waste. Phosphorus is also recovered from wastewater as struvite, and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is now a leading battery chemistry.
contexts.geological: Phosphorus is not found free in nature. It is mined as phosphate rock (apatite), much of it from Morocco and Western Sahara. Phosphate rock carries cadmium, uranium and fluoride as impurities. Phosphorus is on the UK 2024 critical minerals list.
contexts.chemical: Group 15, period 3. White phosphorus is a waxy solid that catches fire on its own in air and is very toxic; red phosphorus is stable and is used on match strikers. In soils and water it is almost always present as phosphate (PO₄³⁻), which binds tightly to iron, aluminium and calcium.
contexts.land: Northern Ireland's farm system brings in more phosphorus, in feed and fertiliser, than it sends out in food. The surplus builds up in soil. The Soil Nutrient Health Scheme has found many fields above the agronomic target index. Fields above the target need no more phosphorus for years, and run-off from them reaches streams.

briefing_text.nature: Phosphate rock (apatite), bones and teeth, soil and manure; never free in nature.
briefing_text.climate: Indirect: fertiliser making uses energy, and phosphorus-rich lakes emit more methane.
briefing_text.pollution: Excess phosphorus causes algal blooms, including in Lough Neagh.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Fertilisers, phosphoric acid, food additives, LFP batteries, flame retardants, pesticides.
briefing_text.health: Essential nutrient; white phosphorus is highly toxic.
briefing_text.hazards: See the phosphorus briefing safety tab.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Hennig Brand in 1669 by boiling down urine, the first element found by a known person; from Greek for 'light-bearer'. Stable.

safety.coshh: COSHH applies to phosphorus and its compounds. White phosphorus is one of the most dangerous elements to handle; it is not something a farm or general workshop should ever hold.
classes: White (yellow) phosphorus
Pyr. Sol. 1 H250 (catches fire spontaneously in air); Acute Tox. 2 H300 + H330 (fatal if swallowed or inhaled); Skin Corr. 1A H314; Aquatic Acute 1 H400. Harmonised (CLP Annex VI).
Red phosphorus
Flam. Sol. 1 H228 (flammable solid); Aquatic Chronic 3 H412. Harmonised (CLP Annex VI).
un: Phosphorus, white or yellow, dry or under water or in solution
safety.risks: White phosphorus ignites in air at around 30 °C, burns deep into skin and is fatal in small doses; it is kept under water. Red phosphorus is far safer but burns easily and can release phosphine if contaminated. Phosphate fertilisers themselves are low hazard to people; the harm is to water.

nature: the mineral in phosphate rock, bones and teeth
the form plants take up and the form that feeds algae
in manure, soil organic matter, DNA and ATP
manufacturing: made from rock and sulfuric acid; fertilisers, food, metal treatment
recovered from wastewater and digestate as a slow-release fertiliser
pesticides such as glyphosate and historic sheep dips
grain fumigant that releases toxic phosphine gas (UN1397)
climate: energy for mining, acid production and transport

elements.name: Sulfur
elements.short: Once acid rain, now a fertiliser crops lack. Hydrogen sulfide from slurry kills; SF₆ in switchgear is the strongest greenhouse gas in common use.

contexts.environmental: Sulfur dioxide from coal and oil caused acid rain and smog. UK emissions fell by 98% between 1970 and 2022, mainly because coal use in power stations ended. Sulfate particles in the air reflect sunlight and cool the climate, so cleaner air has removed some masking of warming. Hydrogen sulfide from slurry is the gas that kills farmers.
contexts.engineering: Most sulfur now comes from cleaning oil and gas, not mining. It is turned into sulfuric acid, the most produced industrial chemical, used for fertilisers, batteries and metal processing. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), an insulating gas in electrical switchgear, is the most potent greenhouse gas regulated under the UNFCCC.
contexts.geological: Sulfur occurs as native sulfur near volcanoes, as sulfides such as pyrite (fool's gold) and galena, and as sulfates such as gypsum. Pyrite exposed to air and water makes acid mine drainage.
contexts.chemical: Group 16, period 3. Spelled 'sulfur' by IUPAC and the Royal Society of Chemistry; 'sulphur' remains common in UK law and HSE guidance. Oxidation states run from −2 (sulfide, H₂S) to +6 (sulfate, sulfuric acid).
contexts.land: With less sulfur falling in rain, many crops and grass silage now need sulfur fertiliser. Sulfur is one of the nutrients reported under Northern Ireland's Soil Nutrient Health Scheme. Gypsum and other sulfates in soil, plasterboard waste and landfill can produce hydrogen sulfide.

briefing_text.nature: Volcanic sulfur, sulfide and sulfate minerals, hydrogen sulfide from bogs and slurry, and dimethyl sulfide from the sea.
briefing_text.climate: Sulfate particles cool the climate; SF₆ is the most potent greenhouse gas in common use.
briefing_text.pollution: Sulfur dioxide caused acid rain; hydrogen sulfide from slurry kills.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Sulfuric acid, fertilisers, vulcanised rubber, gypsum board, batteries.
briefing_text.health: Essential in proteins; SO₂ and H₂S are toxic.
briefing_text.hazards: See the sulfur briefing safety tab.
briefing_text.discovery: Known since antiquity as brimstone; recognised as an element by Lavoisier in 1777. Stable.

safety.coshh: COSHH applies to sulfur and its compounds. On farms, the controlling risk is hydrogen sulfide from slurry: HSENI warns that one breath at high concentration can kill.
classes: Sulfur (element)
Skin Irrit. 2 H315 (causes skin irritation). Harmonised (CLP Annex VI). Sulfur dust is also combustible and can explode.
wels: No specific WEL; general dust limits apply (10 mg/m³ inhalable, 4 mg/m³ respirable)
un: Sulphur (some formed sulphur such as prills or granules may be exempt; check ADR special provision 242)
safety.risks: Solid sulfur is low in toxicity but burns with a blue flame to give choking sulfur dioxide, and its dust can explode. Molten sulfur releases hydrogen sulfide. Hydrogen sulfide deadens the sense of smell at high concentration, so the 'rotten eggs' warning disappears just when it matters.

nature: from slurry, bogs, sewers and volcanoes
released by marine plankton; seeds clouds over the sea
manufacturing: supply sulfur to grass and crops
building material; must be kept separate from biodegradable waste in landfill
climate: cool the climate by reflecting sunlight; their decline has unmasked some warming
100-year global warming potential of 23,500 (AR5) and a lifetime of thousands of years
the global 0.50% sulfur cap from 2020 cut ship SO₂ and some cooling with it

elements.name: Chlorine
elements.short: Disinfects drinking water. Chlorine from CFCs thinned the ozone layer; persistent organochlorines (PCBs, dioxins) build up in food chains.

contexts.environmental: Chlorine from CFCs damaged the ozone layer; chloride from road salt and effluent raises river salinity.
contexts.engineering: Water disinfection, PVC, solvents and pharmaceuticals.
contexts.geological: Found as chloride in seawater and salt deposits.
contexts.chemical: Toxic yellow-green gas; strong oxidiser. Mixing bleach and acid releases it.
contexts.land: Saline soils near coasts; chloride runoff from salted roads.

briefing_text.nature: Chloride in seawater and salt deposits; natural organochlorines are made by some seaweeds and fungi.
briefing_text.climate: Chlorine from CFCs destroyed stratospheric ozone; CFCs are also strong greenhouse gases, now phased out under the Montreal Protocol.
briefing_text.pollution: Persistent organochlorines (DDT, PCBs, dioxins) build up in food chains; chloride from road salt raises river salinity.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Water disinfection, PVC, solvents, pharmaceuticals, bleach; made by electrolysis of brine.
briefing_text.health: Chloride is essential; chlorine gas damages the lungs.
briefing_text.hazards: Chlorine: Press. Gas, Acute Tox. 3 H331, Aquatic Acute 1. Never mix bleach with acid. UN1017.
briefing_text.discovery: Prepared by Carl Scheele in 1774; shown to be an element by Humphry Davy in 1810; from Greek 'chloros', pale green. Stable.

elements.name: Argon
elements.short: Nearly 1% of air; fills double glazing and shields welds. No climate effect; asphyxiant in pits.

contexts.environmental: No climate effect.
contexts.engineering: Shielding gas for welding; filling for double glazing; a by-product of air separation.
contexts.geological: Produced by decay of potassium-40 in rocks.
contexts.chemical: A noble gas: no stable compounds. Asphyxiant in confined spaces.

briefing_text.nature: Nearly 1% of air, made by decay of potassium-40 in rocks over geological time.
briefing_text.climate: No effect.
briefing_text.pollution: None.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Welding shield gas, double-glazing fill, steelmaking, light bulbs.
briefing_text.health: Non-toxic; asphyxiant in confined spaces such as welding pits.
briefing_text.hazards: Heavier than air; collects in low spaces. UN1006 (compressed), UN1951 (refrigerated liquid).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay in 1894; from Greek 'argos', idle. Stable.

elements.name: Potassium
elements.short: Major crop nutrient (potash) and plentiful in slurry. Too much in grass blocks magnesium uptake in livestock.

contexts.environmental: Excess potassium in grass can lock out magnesium in livestock.
contexts.engineering: Potash fertiliser; potassium hydroxide for soaps and batteries.
contexts.geological: Mined as potash from evaporites (for example under North Yorkshire).
contexts.chemical: Very reactive metal; potassium salts are soluble.
contexts.land: Soil K indices guide fertiliser; slurry is rich in potassium.

briefing_text.nature: Feldspars, micas and clays; potash deposits; a major plant nutrient.
briefing_text.climate: Potash mining and fertiliser transport carry energy costs; potassium-40 gives a small natural radioactivity.
briefing_text.pollution: Excess potassium in grass can induce magnesium deficiency in livestock.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Potash fertiliser, potassium hydroxide, soaps, glass.
briefing_text.health: Essential for nerves and muscles; too much or too little affects the heart.
briefing_text.hazards: The metal reacts violently with water (H260). UN2257.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807, his first metal by electrolysis; symbol K from Latin 'kalium'. Stable (potassium-40 is a natural radioactive isotope).

elements.name: Calcium
elements.short: Limestone, chalk and lime. Liming fixes acid soils; cement and lime making release CO₂ and are covered by CBAM.

contexts.environmental: Liming soils and quarrying limestone release CO₂ from carbonate.
contexts.engineering: Cement and lime (CBAM good: cement), plaster, flue-gas desulfurisation.
contexts.geological: Limestone, chalk (the white cliffs of Antrim) and gypsum.
contexts.chemical: Reactive metal; calcium carbonate dissolves in acid.
contexts.land: Lime raises soil pH; most NI grassland soils need lime.

briefing_text.nature: Limestone, chalk, gypsum and shells; bones and teeth. The white cliffs of the Antrim coast are chalk.
briefing_text.climate: Cement and lime making release CO₂ from limestone as well as from fuel; covered by EU and UK CBAM (cement).
briefing_text.pollution: Liming acid soils and lakes reduces aluminium toxicity; quarry dust is a local nuisance.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Cement, lime, plaster, steelmaking flux, flue-gas desulfurisation.
briefing_text.health: Essential for bones; quicklime burns skin and eyes.
briefing_text.hazards: Calcium metal reacts with water (UN1401); quicklime is Skin Irrit. and Eye Dam. 1.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Humphry Davy in 1808; from Latin 'calx', lime. Stable.

elements.name: Scandium
elements.short: Rare metal in light aluminium alloys and fuel cells. No soil, climate or health role of note.

contexts.environmental: Little environmental data.
contexts.engineering: Aluminium-scandium alloys for aerospace; solid oxide fuel cells.
contexts.geological: Dispersed in many ores; recovered as a by-product.

briefing_text.nature: Widely dispersed at low levels; rarely concentrated.
briefing_text.climate: Used in solid oxide fuel cells and light aluminium alloys.
briefing_text.pollution: Little data.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Aluminium-scandium alloys, stadium lighting, fuel cells.
briefing_text.health: Low toxicity data; treated with care as a fine dust.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Lars Nilson in 1879, filling a gap Mendeleev had predicted; named after Scandinavia. Stable.

elements.name: Titanium
elements.short: Light, strong metal; its oxide whitens paint. Titanium dioxide was banned as a food additive in the EU in 2022.

contexts.environmental: Titanium dioxide pigment production generates acidic wastes.
contexts.engineering: Aircraft, implants and desalination plant; TiO₂ is in paints, plastics and sunscreens.
contexts.geological: Ores are ilmenite and rutile, from beach sands and igneous rocks.
contexts.chemical: Protective oxide layer; metal powder is flammable.
contexts.land: Mineral sand mining in coastal areas.

briefing_text.nature: Ilmenite and rutile in igneous rocks and beach sands.
briefing_text.climate: Titanium is light and durable; titanium dioxide production is energy intensive.
briefing_text.pollution: TiO₂ production produces acidic wastes; TiO₂ nanoparticles are studied for effects in water.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Aircraft, implants, desalination plant; TiO₂ whitens paint, plastics, paper and sunscreen.
briefing_text.health: Metal is biocompatible; TiO₂ as a food additive (E171) was banned in the EU in 2022.
briefing_text.discovery: Found by William Gregor in Cornwall in 1791; named by Martin Klaproth after the Titans. Stable.

elements.name: Vanadium
elements.short: Strengthens steel and stores renewable power in flow batteries. Released by burning heavy oil; its pentoxide is a suspected carcinogen.

contexts.environmental: Released from burning heavy fuel oil.
contexts.engineering: High-strength steel; vanadium redox flow batteries for grid storage.
contexts.geological: In magnetite ores and some oil residues; on the 2022 UK critical minerals list.
contexts.chemical: Several oxidation states; vanadium pentoxide is toxic.

briefing_text.nature: In magnetite ores, some shales, crude oil and coal.
briefing_text.climate: Vanadium redox flow batteries store renewable power; vanadium strengthens steel.
briefing_text.pollution: Released by burning heavy fuel oil and coal.
briefing_text.manufacturing: High-strength steel, flow batteries, catalysts for sulfuric acid.
briefing_text.health: Vanadium pentoxide is toxic and a suspected carcinogen.
briefing_text.hazards: Vanadium pentoxide: Muta. 2, Carc. 1B, Repr. 2 (harmonised). UN2862.
briefing_text.discovery: Found in 1801 by Andrés Manuel del Río, rediscovered in 1830 by Nils Sefström; named after Vanadís (Freyja). Stable.

elements.name: Chromium
elements.short: Makes steel stainless. Hexavalent chromium from plating and tanning is a carcinogen and a contaminated-land priority.

contexts.environmental: Hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) is carcinogenic and a contaminated-land priority.
contexts.engineering: Stainless steel, plating and tanning.
contexts.chemical: Cr(III) is a trace nutrient; Cr(VI) is toxic and mobile in water.
contexts.land: Old tanneries, plating works and chromite-ore residues leave contaminated sites.

briefing_text.nature: Chromite ore; small amounts in most soils.
briefing_text.climate: Essential to stainless steel used in energy plant.
briefing_text.pollution: Hexavalent chromium from plating, tanning and pigments is a priority contaminant in water and land.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Stainless steel, plating, leather tanning, pigments.
briefing_text.health: Chromium(III) is a trace nutrient; chromium(VI) causes lung cancer and skin ulcers.
briefing_text.hazards: Chromium(VI) compounds: Carc. 1B, skin sensitiser; strict WELs.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797; from Greek 'chroma', colour. Stable.

elements.name: Manganese
elements.short: Steel and battery metal and a plant micronutrient. Dissolves in waterlogged and peaty ground, staining water supplies.

contexts.environmental: Manganese dissolves in waterlogged soils and peaty water, staining supplies.
contexts.engineering: Steel deoxidiser; battery cathodes.
contexts.geological: Manganese oxides and nodules on the ocean floor.
contexts.chemical: Many oxidation states; permanganate is a strong oxidiser.
contexts.land: Deficiency in limed, high-organic soils; toxicity in acid wet soils.

briefing_text.nature: Manganese oxides in rocks and soils; nodules on the ocean floor.
briefing_text.climate: Used in steel and in battery cathodes.
briefing_text.pollution: Dissolves in waterlogged soils and peaty water, staining supplies and blocking pipes.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Steelmaking, aluminium cans, batteries, fertiliser micronutrient.
briefing_text.health: Essential trace nutrient; chronic exposure to fume (welding, mining) affects the nervous system.
briefing_text.hazards: Manganese and inorganic compounds WEL 0.2 mg/m³ inhalable, 0.05 mg/m³ respirable (EH40).
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Johan Gottlieb Gahn in 1774; name from magnesia nigra. Stable.

elements.name: Iron
elements.short: Steel: a major CO₂ source and a CBAM good. Iron binds phosphate in soil; ochre from old mines smothers streams.

contexts.environmental: Blast-furnace steelmaking is a major CO₂ source; scrap and hydrogen routes cut it.
contexts.engineering: Structural steel, reinforcement, machinery. Iron and steel are covered by EU and UK CBAM.
contexts.geological: Haematite and magnetite ores; laterite iron ores formed between the Antrim lavas.
contexts.chemical: Rusts in air and water; iron binds phosphate in soils.
contexts.land: Ochre in drains and streams from iron-rich groundwater and old mines.

briefing_text.nature: Fourth most abundant element in the crust; haematite and magnetite ores, and the Earth's core.
briefing_text.climate: Blast-furnace steel is a major CO₂ source; scrap-based and hydrogen routes cut it. Iron and steel are covered by EU and UK CBAM.
briefing_text.pollution: Iron ochre from old mines and iron-rich drains smothers stream beds.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Steel for construction, vehicles and machinery; cast iron.
briefing_text.health: Essential for blood; iron overdose is dangerous to children.
briefing_text.hazards: Iron powder can be flammable; metal is not classified.
briefing_text.discovery: Used since about 1200 BC (the Iron Age); symbol Fe from Latin 'ferrum'. Stable.

elements.name: Cobalt
elements.short: Battery and turbine metal with hard supply chains. Trace nutrient for sheep (cobalt 'pine'); some compounds are carcinogens.

contexts.environmental: Mining in some regions raises human-rights and pollution concerns.
contexts.engineering: Lithium-ion cathodes, jet-engine superalloys, magnets.
contexts.geological: Mostly a by-product of copper and nickel mining; on the UK critical minerals list.
contexts.chemical: Vitamin B12 contains cobalt; some cobalt compounds are carcinogens.
contexts.land: Cobalt-deficient pasture causes 'pine' in sheep; supplemented in minerals.

briefing_text.nature: With copper and nickel ores; traces in soils.
briefing_text.climate: Used in battery cathodes and superalloys for turbines.
briefing_text.pollution: Mining in some regions brings serious human-rights and pollution concerns.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Batteries, jet-engine superalloys, magnets, catalysts, blue pigments.
briefing_text.health: Part of vitamin B12; some cobalt compounds are carcinogens.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Georg Brandt in about 1735; from German 'Kobold', a goblin of the mines. Stable.

elements.name: Nickel
elements.short: Stainless steel and battery metal. A common skin allergen; smelting releases sulfur dioxide.

contexts.environmental: Nickel refining emits sulfur dioxide; nickel is a common contact allergen.
contexts.engineering: Stainless steel, plating, battery cathodes.
contexts.land: Ultramafic soils are naturally rich in nickel.

briefing_text.nature: Laterite and sulfide ores; ultramafic soils.
briefing_text.climate: Nickel-rich cathodes give batteries more range; nickel mining can clear forest.
briefing_text.pollution: Smelting releases sulfur dioxide and metal dust.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Stainless steel, batteries, plating, coins.
briefing_text.health: A common skin allergen; some nickel compounds are carcinogens.
briefing_text.discovery: Isolated by Axel Cronstedt in 1751; from German 'Kupfernickel', devil's copper. Stable.

elements.name: Copper
elements.short: Wiring for electrification. Toxic to aquatic life; builds up in soils from pig slurry and fungicides; too much poisons sheep.

contexts.environmental: Toxic to aquatic life; copper fungicides and antifouling build up in soils and sediments.
contexts.engineering: Electrical cables, motors, heat exchangers. Demand rises with electrification.
contexts.geological: Porphyry and sulfide ores; historic mining in Ireland, including Avoca.
contexts.chemical: Good conductor; copper salts are toxic to fungi and algae.
contexts.land: Trace nutrient for livestock; pig slurry can raise soil copper.

briefing_text.nature: Copper sulfide and oxide ores; traces in soil and food.
briefing_text.climate: Demand rises with electrification: cables, motors, renewables.
briefing_text.pollution: Toxic to aquatic life; copper fungicides and antifouling paint build up in soils and sediments.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Wiring, plumbing, motors, heat exchangers, brass and bronze.
briefing_text.health: Essential trace nutrient; too much is toxic, especially to sheep.
briefing_text.hazards: Copper powder: Aquatic hazards. Massive metal not classified.
briefing_text.discovery: Used since about 9000 BC; symbol Cu from Latin 'cuprum', from Cyprus. Stable.

elements.name: Zinc
elements.short: Galvanises steel. Washes off roofs and roads into drains, harming aquatic life; an essential nutrient for people and stock.

contexts.environmental: Washes off galvanised and roofing surfaces into drains; toxic to aquatic life.
contexts.engineering: Galvanising, die-casting, brass, batteries.
contexts.geological: Sphalerite ore; Ireland's Tara mine is one of Europe's largest zinc mines.
contexts.chemical: Essential trace nutrient; zinc oxide is used in creams and rubber.
contexts.land: Pig slurry and sewage sludge can raise soil zinc.

briefing_text.nature: Sphalerite ore; Ireland's Tara mine is among Europe's largest.
briefing_text.climate: Galvanising extends the life of steel; zinc batteries are researched for storage.
briefing_text.pollution: Runoff from galvanised roofs and roads; toxic to aquatic life.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Galvanising, die-casting, brass, rubber, sunscreen.
briefing_text.health: Essential trace nutrient; zinc fume causes 'metal fume fever'.
briefing_text.hazards: Zinc powder (stabilised): Aquatic Acute/Chronic 1 (harmonised); powder reacts with water (UN1436).
briefing_text.discovery: Used in brass since antiquity; isolated in Europe by Andreas Marggraf in 1746. Stable.

elements.name: Gallium
elements.short: Makes efficient LEDs and power electronics. A critical mineral with exports controlled by China; no soil or climate role.

contexts.environmental: Little environmental concern at current use.
contexts.engineering: Gallium nitride LEDs and power electronics; gallium arsenide chips.
contexts.geological: By-product of aluminium and zinc refining; on the UK critical minerals list.
contexts.chemical: Liquid just above room temperature; attacks aluminium.

briefing_text.nature: Very dispersed; recovered as a by-product of bauxite and zinc processing.
briefing_text.climate: Gallium nitride makes efficient LEDs and power electronics for chargers, inverters and EVs.
briefing_text.pollution: Little environmental concern at present use.
briefing_text.manufacturing: LEDs, radio-frequency chips, power electronics, solar cells. On the UK critical minerals list; China dominates supply and controls exports.
briefing_text.health: Low toxicity; some compounds used in medicine.
briefing_text.hazards: Liquid just above room temperature; corrodes aluminium (UN2803). Metal is Skin Corr./Eye Dam. by many suppliers.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1875, as Mendeleev predicted; named after Gallia (France). Stable.

elements.name: Germanium
elements.short: Fibre optics and satellite solar cells. Little environmental concern; supply controlled by China.

contexts.environmental: Little environmental concern.
contexts.engineering: Fibre optics, infrared lenses, solar cells for satellites.
contexts.geological: By-product of zinc and coal; supply concentrated.

briefing_text.nature: Traces in zinc ores and some coals.
briefing_text.climate: Used in high-efficiency solar cells for satellites and in infrared optics.
briefing_text.pollution: Little concern.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Fibre-optic glass, infrared lenses, PET catalyst in some regions, semiconductors. Export controls apply in China.
briefing_text.health: Low toxicity; some 'germanium supplements' have caused kidney damage.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Clemens Winkler in 1886; named after Germany. Stable.

elements.name: Arsenic
elements.short: Natural in some groundwater and a legacy of sheep dip and timber treatment. A carcinogen in drinking water and a contaminated-land priority.

contexts.environmental: Arsenic in groundwater is a major global health problem; also from old pesticides and timber treatment.
contexts.engineering: Semiconductors (gallium arsenide); historic wood preservative (CCA).
contexts.geological: In sulfide ores and some sedimentary rocks.
contexts.land: Old sheep-dip, timber-treatment and mine sites can be contaminated.

briefing_text.nature: In sulfide ores, some shales and groundwater; naturally high in groundwater in parts of South Asia.
briefing_text.climate: No direct role; gallium arsenide is used in some solar cells.
briefing_text.pollution: Arsenic in drinking water is a major global health problem; also from old pesticides, wood preservative (CCA), mining and smelting.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Semiconductors, historic pesticides and timber treatment, lead alloys.
briefing_text.health: Inorganic arsenic causes cancers and skin lesions; drinking-water limit 10 µg/l.
briefing_text.hazards: Arsenic compounds: Acute Tox. 3, Carc. 1A. Arsine gas is extremely toxic (UN2188). UN1558 (arsenic).
briefing_text.discovery: Known in antiquity; isolated by Albertus Magnus in about 1250. Stable.

elements.name: Selenium
elements.short: Trace nutrient many UK and Irish soils lack, so livestock are supplemented. Toxic in excess to birds and fish.

contexts.environmental: Selenium-poor soils give low-selenium grass; excess is toxic to birds and fish.
contexts.engineering: Glass decolouriser, electronics, photovoltaics.
contexts.geological: Associated with sulfide minerals and some shales.
contexts.land: Many UK and Irish soils are low in selenium; livestock are supplemented.

briefing_text.nature: With sulfide minerals; soils vary widely; many UK and Irish soils are low.
briefing_text.climate: Used in some thin-film solar cells (CIGS).
briefing_text.pollution: Selenium from coal ash and irrigation drainage has poisoned birds and fish.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Glass decolouriser, electronics, pigments, feed supplements.
briefing_text.health: Essential trace nutrient with a narrow line between deficiency and toxicity.
briefing_text.hazards: Selenium and compounds: Acute Tox. 3, STOT RE 2. UN2658 (selenium powder).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Berzelius in 1817; named after Selene, the Moon. Stable.

elements.name: Bromine
elements.short: Halons and methyl bromide destroyed ozone; some brominated flame retardants persist in the environment.

contexts.environmental: Bromine from halons and methyl bromide depletes ozone; some brominated flame retardants are persistent pollutants.
contexts.engineering: Flame retardants, drilling fluids, water treatment.
contexts.land: Methyl bromide soil fumigation is now banned in the UK and EU.

briefing_text.nature: Bromide in seawater and brines; seaweeds make natural organobromines.
briefing_text.climate: Bromine from halons and methyl bromide destroys stratospheric ozone more efficiently than chlorine.
briefing_text.pollution: Some brominated flame retardants are persistent organic pollutants; bromate forms when bromide-rich water is ozonated.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Flame retardants, drilling fluids, water treatment, pharmaceuticals.
briefing_text.health: Bromine liquid and vapour burn skin and lungs.
briefing_text.hazards: Bromine: Acute Tox. 2 H330, Skin Corr. 1A. UN1744.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered independently by Antoine Balard (1826) and Carl Löwig (1825); from Greek 'bromos', stench. Stable.

elements.name: Krypton
elements.short: Inert gas filling high-performance glazing. No climate or soil effect.

contexts.environmental: No climate effect.
contexts.engineering: Fills high-performance double and triple glazing; lighting.
contexts.chemical: A noble gas; forms very few compounds.

briefing_text.nature: Trace gas in air (about 1 part per million).
briefing_text.climate: Fills high-performance glazing to cut heat loss.
briefing_text.pollution: Krypton-85 from nuclear reprocessing is released at low levels.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Insulating glass units, lighting, lasers; by-product of air separation.
briefing_text.health: Non-toxic; asphyxiant.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Ramsay and Travers in 1898; from Greek 'kryptos', hidden. Stable.

elements.name: Rubidium
elements.short: Used in atomic clocks. No environmental role of note.

contexts.environmental: No significant environmental role.
contexts.engineering: Atomic clocks and research.
contexts.geological: Trace in potassium minerals; rubidium–strontium dating of rocks.

briefing_text.nature: Traces in potassium minerals and seawater.
briefing_text.climate: No significant role.
briefing_text.pollution: None of note.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Atomic clocks (used in GPS), research, specialist glass.
briefing_text.health: Low toxicity; behaves like potassium in the body.
briefing_text.hazards: Metal ignites in air and reacts violently with water (UN1423).
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Bunsen and Kirchhoff in 1861 by spectroscopy; from Latin 'rubidus', deep red. Stable (rubidium-87 is weakly radioactive).

elements.name: Strontium
elements.short: Follows calcium into bone. Radioactive strontium-90 from fallout is the concern; stable strontium is low risk.

contexts.environmental: Strontium-90 from nuclear fallout is a radiological concern; stable strontium is low risk.
contexts.engineering: Fireworks, flares, ferrite magnets.
contexts.geological: Celestine and strontianite (named after Strontian, Scotland).

briefing_text.nature: Celestine and strontianite; follows calcium in shells and bones.
briefing_text.climate: No direct role.
briefing_text.pollution: Strontium-90 from fallout and nuclear accidents is a radiological concern; stable strontium is low risk.
briefing_text.manufacturing: Red fireworks and flares, ferrite magnets, toothpaste for sensitive teeth.

elements.name: Radon
elements.short: Radioactive gas from the ground; the main radiation dose in UK homes and a cause of lung cancer. Airtight retrofits can trap it.

contexts.environmental: Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps from the ground into buildings. Breathing its decay products over years raises the risk of lung cancer, especially for smokers. Outdoors it disperses harmlessly; indoors it can build up.
contexts.engineering: Radon protection in new buildings uses a gas-resistant membrane, with a sump or ventilated sub-floor in higher-risk areas. Existing buildings are fixed with a radon sump and fan or better under-floor ventilation. Making buildings more airtight to save energy can raise indoor radon unless ventilation is designed in.
contexts.geological: Radon-222 comes from the decay of uranium in rocks and soils, via radium. Levels follow geology; Northern Ireland's radon potential map (UKHSA, GSNI and BGS) shows the areas affected. Radon also dissolves in groundwater, so private wells can carry it.
contexts.chemical: Group 18, period 6; the heaviest naturally occurring noble gas. Chemically almost inert. Radon-222 has a half-life of 3.8 days and decays through short-lived polonium, lead and bismuth isotopes that stick to dust and lodge in the lungs.
contexts.land: Whether a site is in a radon affected area decides what protection a new building needs under the Building Regulations (Northern Ireland). Workplaces in affected areas should test, and employers must act where annual averages exceed 300 Bq/m³ under the Ionising Radiations Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2017.

briefing_text.nature: Seeps from uranium-bearing rocks and soil; dissolves in groundwater.
briefing_text.climate: Not a greenhouse gas; used as a tracer of land air; airtight retrofits can raise indoor levels.
briefing_text.pollution: Indoor radon is the main source of radiation dose to most people in the UK.
briefing_text.manufacturing: No industrial use of note.
briefing_text.health: Long-term exposure causes lung cancer, especially in smokers.
briefing_text.hazards: See the radon briefing safety tab.
briefing_text.discovery: Discovered by Friedrich Ernst Dorn in 1900. No stable isotope; radon-222 half-life 3.8 days.

safety.coshh: COSHH does not cover the radiation hazard of radon; the Ionising Radiations Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2017 do. Radioactive substances also fall outside CLP classification.
